before: A generic type uses a type parameter as a placeholder. In Box<T>, T stands for the item type chosen by code that uses the class.
Box<int> uses int for T; Box<string> uses string. The constructor receives a T value and stores it in a read-only Item property. The get-only property can be assigned by the constructor.

An integer box expects an integer item. Supplying quoted text to new Box<int> is a type mismatch, not an automatic conversion. A generic definition avoids writing a separate box class for every item type.
Expected behavior from this example: 5 then map. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Create Box<bool> with true and print its Item without changing the generic class. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A generic type has a place for a type chosen by its caller. In Box<T>, T is a type parameter: the placeholder for the item type.
Box<int> chooses int for T. Box<string> chooses string. The constructor receives that kind of item and stores it in Item.
Choosing a type keeps type checking in place. An integer box expects an integer. It does not automatically turn quoted text into a number.
The program prints 5, then map. The number box holds 4, so adding one gives 5. The text box holds map.
The same Box definition works for both item types. Item is a get-only property: this constructor can set it, but calling code cannot assign a replacement.

before.explanation: Choosing Box<int> makes its constructor input an int. Quoted "7" is a string; the generic placeholder does not disable checking or parse that text.

after.question: Pass the text "7" to new Box<int> instead of the number 4. What happens?
choices: Compilation fails because the constructor expects an int.
T allows any value without checking.
after.explanation: Box<int> requires an int item. Quoted text has type string, so it does not match.
